We are a group of students from Germinare TECH (Instituto J&F), with members who work at companies such as JBS and PicPay. Our backgrounds include Systems Analysis and Development, RPA, BI, Java, Spring Boot, mobile development, AI agents, LangChain, LangGraph, Claude Code, statistics, and ETL.

summary: PyroSync turns NASA's two active-fire records into one. MODIS has detected fires since 2001 and VIIRS since 2012, but they do not see fire the same way, and NASA projects the end of MODIS science in 2027. PyroSync converts the MODIS years into VIIRS-equivalent weekly counts and publishes a burning activity calendar from 2001 to 2026 for five regions on five continents: Pantanal, Iberia, Southern Africa, Indonesia and Northern Australia. For any area a user draws inside a region, it shows the historical pattern, the weeks that were unusual for that time of year, and the critical period of the fire season. Every conversion is tested one year at a time against a simple baseline, and each region shows whether it passed: three did, two are labelled as baseline. A one-page briefing in English and Portuguese serves land managers; a CSV export and the validation panel serve scientists. Its companion, PyroSync Atlas, watches the whole planet in near real time with NASA FIRMS, so responders can see today's detections and read them against 26 years of history.
details:
What it does. PyroSync is a web application that harmonizes the MODIS (Terra and Aqua, Collection 6.1) and VIIRS (S-NPP, 375 m) active fire records from NASA FIRMS into one weekly burning activity calendar, 2001 to 2026. It opens on the planet with five regions on five continents; choosing one flies to it. Inside a region the user can play through 26 years, select an area of interest, and see its calendar, its unusual weeks (above the 90th percentile for that week of the year), its critical period (the weeks that hold 80% of a typical year), yearly totals, the detections on the globe and a sonification of the season.

How it works. A Python pipeline pairs MODIS and VIIRS detections in the overlap years, fits a model that converts MODIS weekly counts into VIIRS-equivalent counts with an uncertainty band, and validates it by leaving one year out at a time against a simple monthly-ratio baseline. A region where the model does not beat the baseline is shown as "baseline", not hidden: the conversion passed in three of the five regions. Weeks without data stay gaps and are never shown as zero. Everything is precomputed and served as static files, so the site needs no server.

Who it is for. Land managers get a printable one-page briefing in English and Portuguese. Scientists get a CSV export, the validation figures and the method. Responders get PyroSync Atlas, our companion app: a worldwide near-real-time monitor of NASA FIRMS detections with monthly history maps, an experimental next-day model and plain-language summaries that cite their sources.

What is creative. Every estimate is shown next to its own track record: the alert rule comes with its hits, late calls, misses and false alarms over 25 past seasons, and every region says whether its conversion passed validation. The fire season can also be heard, week by week.

Limits. Counts are satellite detections, not burned area or risk. Wildfires and agricultural burns are both counted and not told apart. The alert rule is tested retrospectively on data that ends on 11 November 2026. PyroSync Atlas shows direct, non-harmonized detections and its forecast is experimental.

Tools. PyroSync: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), JavaScript with Vite, deck.gl and Tone.js, published on GitHub Pages. PyroSync Atlas: React, TypeScript, CesiumJS and FastAPI. Code: https://github.com/os-fiscal-de-rejunte/fireseam-modis-viirs-harmonizer and https://github.com/os-fiscal-de-rejunte/pyrosync-atlas. Live atlas: https://pyrosync-api.onrender.com/
